report:
**Conclusion: The claim is well-supported by the evidence.**

Multiple studies and systematic reviews confirm that bystander hands-only (compression-only) CPR is associated with greater survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) compared to no bystander CPR.

A nationwide observational study found that "after multivariable adjustment, both types of bystander CPR were associated with higher survival, as compared to patients with no bystander" CPR, directly supporting the survival benefit of hands-only CPR specifically ([PMC9803815](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9803815/)). A study highlighted by the American Heart Association stated that "doing only chest compressions doubles the chance of survival, compared to doing nothing" ([Emergency Live](https://www.emergency-live.com/health-and-safety/survive-an-ohca-the-american-heart-association-revealed-that-hands-only-cpr-increases-survival-rate/)). A recent PubMed-indexed study similarly noted that "CPR for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest is associated with higher survival" and examined time-to-bystander-CPR thresholds compared with no bystander CPR ([PubMed 40015622](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40015622/)).

The ILCOR Consensus on Science review cited Sasson et al. (2010), a systematic review and meta-analysis, concluding that "bystander CPR more than doubles OHCA survival" ([ILCOR CoSTR](https://costr.ilcor.org/document/dispatcher-assisted-compression-only-cpr-compared-with-conventional-cpr-in-adults-bls-2112-tf-sr)). Duke University reporting reinforced this, noting bystander CPR "doubles the chance of survival" ([Duke Medicine](https://medschool.duke.edu/news/no-matter-where-they-live-women-are-less-likely-get-bystander-cpr)).

The evidence is observational rather than randomized (ethical constraints preclude withholding CPR), but it is consistent across large nationwide cohorts and meta-analyses. Hands-only CPR also reduces barriers to bystander intervention, which may further amplify its public-health benefit.
